newsitem.title: USA: Business group says U.S. wage costs rising in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Business group says U.S. wage costs rising in 1997.

text.p: The proportion of U.S. companies reporting rising wage costs climbed to the highest level since 1990 in the first three months of this year, The National Association of Business Economists (NABE) said on Wednesday.
A survey of 123 NABE member companies found 45.5 percent said that their wage and salary costs had grown in the first quarter, a sharp increase from 35.7 percent in the final quarter of last year.
NABE said it was the highest level reporting rising wage costs since 1990.

Though 25 percent of respondents said that raw material costs rose in the first quarter, on balance NABE said that prices were "exceptionally well-behaved, especially for an economy entering its seventh year of expansion."
Only about one-quarter of the survey respondents said they had increased their prices for finished products -- and 30 percent were unable to make the full price increase stick.
"Another 22 percent failed to realize any price increase at all, reflecting a very competitive business environment," NABE said.
The survey found that business conditions were robust, but slightly less so than in the closing quarter of last year.

"Overall, demand for respondent firms products and services continued to grow but at a slower pace than in the strong fourth quarter," NABE said. Manufacturing industries, though, said their demand was up significantly in the first three months this year.
Hiring plans were "very strong" among busy goods producers but companies generally said that job growth was not as brisk in this year's first quarter as during the final quarter of 1996.

Nearly half the NABE members who sell abroad said they boosted their exports during the first quarter but the rising value of the U.S. dollar was making it "progressively more difficult" to sell overseas.
A costlier dollar relative to other currencies makes U.S. products more expensive for foreigners to buy while it simultaneously makes imports cheaper.
"Overall, the stronger dollar is having a negative impact on half the responding manufacturing firms," NABE said. "For other types of firms, there has been no appreciable impact."

Businesses continued to spend heavily to increase their production facilities and to buy new machinery to produce more goods. NABE said that 44.4 percent of survey respondents were spending more on capital goods.
"This growth in capital spending matches the level reached in 1994 and was exceeded only twice in the last 11 years," NABE said.
